An equal payment plan smooths cash, not cost: track the credit before you treat it as money

Follow a fictional twelve-period utility ledger to separate a total charge, a billed installment, cash actually paid and the running difference, then test an installment recomputation and a separate refund without double counting.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 8 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Track an equal payment plan against the charges it is smoothing

Interactive planning lab

Fictional total charges for the twelve periods$2,000
Cash paid through the twelve installments$1,800
Charges minus cash paid at the year end$200
Recomputed installment after the selected month$183.33

An original twelve-period teaching ledger with fictional monthly total charges and one paid installment per period. It is not a BC Hydro, FortisBC or any other provider invoice, tariff or annual reconciliation statement. Each entered charge is already the complete fictional cost assigned to that period, so no tax, rebate, deposit, late fee, interest or meter correction is added. The running difference is charges minus cash paid: a positive value means cumulative charges exceed cumulative cash paid and a negative value means a modeled credit. It is not the provider’s amount due, an arrears balance, approved borrowing, an available refund or spendable bank cash. The annuity-style recomputation divides the current signed difference plus forecast remaining charges by the remaining months and assumes those forecasts are realized exactly and every installment arrives on time. It is not a provider adjustment formula or a right to choose an installment. A separate hypothetical refund is capped at an existing modeled credit and returns previously paid cash; it is not income, and the same credit must not also be carried forward. No reduction in the underlying charges, coverage of a shortfall, payment arrangement or collection outcome is modeled, and no current tariff, actual account or usage recommendation is supplied.

The central idea

A level installment changes when cash leaves the household. The charges it is smoothing remain separate, and a negative running difference is an unsettled credit rather than spendable cash or a promised refund.

01

Separate the timing of cash from the cost of the service

An equal payment plan asks a household to pay a similar amount each month instead of following a seasonal bill. That is a cash-flow arrangement. It does not make the electricity, gas or water delivered across the year cost the same in every month.

BC Hydro’s customer-service rules describe a monthly installment based on the preceding year’s use, reviewed periodically and changed when needed. The anniversary bill compares the installments billed with the year’s actual use, producing a credit when use was lower and an additional charge when it was higher. FortisBC’s equal payment plan describes a similar smoothing idea with its own review periods, and separates how natural gas and electricity reviews work.

Two details in those descriptions matter for any household budget. First, the review cadence and the anniversary treatment are provider-specific, so one utility’s rule cannot be imported into another’s plan. Second, an installment is a requested planned payment, not proof that cash moved. BC Hydro’s payment page lists equal payments separately from pre-authorized withdrawals and notes that online-banking payments can take several business days to appear.

The ledger in this article is therefore deliberately generic. It uses twelve complete charge periods and twelve paid installments, and it does not reproduce either provider’s anniversary invoice.

02

Keep four quantities apart before doing any arithmetic

Most confusion about equal payments comes from collapsing four different numbers into one.

The actual charge is the total cost assigned to a period’s service. In this example it is known exactly, because it is authored. In a real household an estimate, a forecast or an interim meter read is not a final charge.

The installment billed is the amount the provider asks for. It is a request, not a receipt. The cash paid is what actually reached the provider in the period. The running difference is cumulative charges minus cumulative cash paid. A positive value means charges recognized so far exceed cash paid so far; a negative value is a modeled credit.

Two further numbers stay outside that equation. The amount due or arrears is what the provider states is payable, with its own deadline. A refund is a separate return of cash already paid. Neither is produced automatically by the sign of the running difference.

Write the balance as opening difference + this period’s charge − this period’s cash paid. Keeping that structure prevents a charge from being counted twice when an installment is paid, and prevents missing data from being silently treated as zero.

03

Read a twelve-period ledger where the credit arrives before the cost

The example below uses an authored pattern of monthly charges totalling CAD 2,000 and a constant CAD 150 installment, so cash paid totals CAD 1,800 over the twelve periods.

Early periods run a credit: charges of CAD 90 against CAD 150 paid produce a difference of negative CAD 60, and the modeled credit deepens to negative CAD 160 by the fourth period. The high-charge periods then absorb it. The balance turns positive in the seventh period and peaks at CAD 270 in the tenth.

The plan ends with CAD 200 of charges not yet covered by the twelve assumed payments. A separate hypothetical settlement of CAD 200 would clear it. Presenting CAD 2,000 of charges and CAD 2,000 of installments plus settlement as two expenses would count the same service twice.

Notice what the ledger has and has not shown. It has shown the size and direction of the timing gap at each period end. It has not shown a missed payment, a late fee, a demand for immediate payment or an approved refund, because none of those events is in the model.

04

Treat a credit as an unsettled balance, not as savings

A negative running difference is the point where budgets most often go wrong. If a household has paid more than the charges recognized so far, the money has left its account. It sits with the provider as an unsettled balance. It is not available to spend, transfer or invest, and it is not yet a refund.

Conversely, a positive running difference during the plan is normally the intended effect of smoothing: the household has used service it has not yet finished paying for. It is not automatically overdue, a borrowing facility or a collection matter. Only the provider’s own statement can establish what is due and when.

This is also why an equal-payment credit should never be listed beside an emergency reserve. The reserve is cash the household can deploy today. The credit is a claim whose timing, amount and form depend on the provider’s reconciliation and its own terms. BC Hydro’s bill explanation shows the current and overdue amounts, payment dates, payments made and an equal-payment tracker as distinct fields for exactly this reason.

When a household wants a cash buffer for seasonal bills, the right instrument is money it actually holds. A plan that spreads the provider’s charges does something different, and the two should not be added together as if they were the same asset.

05

Recompute the installment with an explicit, inspectable formula

Plans are reviewed, and the installment can change. A transparent way to illustrate that is to divide the current signed difference plus forecast remaining charges by the number of remaining periods.

After the sixth period the charges total CAD 870 and cash paid totals CAD 900, so the difference is negative CAD 30. Forecast charges for the remaining six periods are CAD 1,130. The recomputed installment is (−30 + 1,130) ÷ 6 = CAD 183.33, with a final period adjusted by two cents if the plan is settled to the cent.

Three limits belong beside that arithmetic. It assumes the forecast is realized exactly. It assumes every installment arrives on time. And it is an illustration, not a provider’s adjustment algorithm or a household’s right to select an installment.

If the formula produces a negative payment, the model has produced a credit to resolve separately. Automatic negative transfers do not exist, and no refund should be promised from that sign alone.

The chart keeps both paths visible: the constant installment and the recomputed one. Their endpoints differ only because the cash schedule changed. The charges do not move.

06

Changing the installment and changing the charge are separate experiments

Lowering the installment raises the year-end difference almost dollar for dollar and leaves the charges untouched. Raising it reduces the difference but commits more current household cash. Neither action changes what the service cost.

Cost sensitivity is a different experiment. Applying a ten percent multiplier to every fictional total charge raises the annual total to CAD 2,200. Holding CAD 150 installments leaves CAD 400 uncovered instead of CAD 200. That is a total-charge scenario, not a tariff change or a measured usage response.

A simple bill identity helps keep the two apart. If a charge equals a fixed component plus a unit price multiplied by quantity, then price and quantity move the variable part while the fixed component stays fixed. Actual tiered rates, time-of-day pricing, taxes and other line items are outside that identity, so the model does not claim that equal billing locks either the price or the consumption.

The matrix in the charts crosses several installments with three charge multipliers. Read each cell as a year-end difference under stated assumptions. It is not a saving, an arrears forecast or evidence about any provider’s behaviour.

07

Resolve an ending credit once, not twice

Suppose the household instead paid CAD 175 each period. Cash paid becomes CAD 2,100 and the plan ends with a modeled credit of CAD 100. The running balance still turns positive in the ninth and tenth periods, peaking at CAD 25, which shows that an ending credit does not prove the household was ahead at every earlier date.

There are two clean ways to resolve that credit, and only one should be recorded. A separate refund of CAD 100 returns previously advanced cash and brings the difference to zero. Alternatively the credit is carried into later service and reduces the next amount to fund.

Keeping the credit and also counting a cash refund is the double count to avoid. So is treating the refund as new income: it restores cash the household had already paid, so it does not improve the year’s net position.

The model caps any entered refund at the credit that actually exists, and shows the refund as a separate step in the year-end reconciliation. Provider-specific refund timing, closure rules and any interest treatment are outside the example and must be read from the provider’s current terms.

08

Verify the real account with the real document

A teaching ledger cannot tell a household what its own utility will do. When an equal payment plan matters to a real budget, read the current bill and the provider’s own explanation of it.

Check which figure is the installment and which is the amount actually due. Check whether the payment shown has posted or is still in transit. Look for the plan tracker and any anniversary comparison, and note the period those figures cover. Confirm the review date the provider states rather than assuming a calendar year.

Then check the treatment of any credit. Is it being carried forward, refunded on request, or applied only at closure? A general description of a plan is not a statement about a specific account, and a credit balance is not an emergency fund.

Finally, keep the household’s own cash record separate from the provider’s balance. The household record answers what left the bank account. The provider record answers what has been charged and reconciled. Reconciling the two occasionally is what turns a smoothed payment into a budget that can be explained.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Six original charts use one authored seasonal charge pattern and invented installments. No current tariff, actual account, measured consumption, weather data, provider invoice formula or recommendation about usage is shown. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. BC Hydro · Customer service rules, equal payment plan and closed-account credit ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026. Used for the installment basis on prior use, periodic review, the anniversary comparison of billed installments with actual use, and the separate treatment of a credit remaining after account closure. No current tariff, rate or actual account is reproduced. The page is mutable customer information, so the review date is not treated as its publication date.

  2. FortisBC · Equal Payment Plan ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026. Used only to establish that a second provider describes its own review cadence and separate natural-gas and electricity reconciliation treatments. No FortisBC rule is imported into the BC Hydro description or into the model.

    Reviewed 25 October 2026. Used for the distinction between an equal payment plan, pre-authorized withdrawals and online-banking payments that can take several business days to appear. No payment timing is modeled as a guarantee.

  4. BC Hydro · Understanding your bill ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026. Used for the separation of current and overdue amounts, payment dates, payments made and the equal-payment tracker. The model’s signed running difference is an authored teaching quantity, not a reproduction of those fields.
